title: AP exams
text:
Gunn Wiki article: AP exams

The Advanced Placement examinations (AP exams) are an annual occurrence at many high schools in the US, including Gunn High School. The AP exams are an important component of Gunn culture to demonstrate one's proficiency to colleges and possibly gain college credit, which can be used to reduce tuition fees.

Structure:
The structure of AP exams vary significantly depending on the subject of the exam. Most exams have multiple choice and free response sections, usually taking 2–3 hours.

Due to school closures during the Covid-19 pandemic, the AP exam format was temporarily changed to allow the test to be taken virtually. However, because the new temporary tests were significantly shorter, the ability of these exams to accurately reflect the student's understanding of a course has been contested.

title: AP exams
text:
porary tests were significantly shorter, the ability of these exams to accurately reflect the student's understanding of a course has been contested.

A list of materials needed for the test is available on College Board's website. However, students generally need to bring two pencils and pens to the test; pencil is required for the multiple choice section which is completed by Scantron. Mechanical pencils are not allowed since their lead may fail to register on the Scantron.

The exam structure is very rigid because of College Board's desire to avoid any cheating or unfair advantages. Students may only bring their materials to their desks and must leave backpacks by the wall. A short break is allowed between the multiple-choice and free-response sections in which students are confined to a small area around the exam room. They are told not to talk about the exam or the exam subject, though this is not strictly enforced. 

Registration:
At Gunn, registration is only accepted from PAUSD students due to space constraints, especially with COVID.

also enroll on AP Classroom. Teachers may use AP Classroom to provide resources to students as practice in-class or out of class.

Grading:
Multiple choice questions are graded on a binary scale, solely on the number of correct answers.

Free response questions have strict scoring criteria to prevent grader bias. Each part of a question is generally 2-5 points, with 1 point awarded per feature in the response. These features can range from having a very specific thing written down to implying a certain general idea.

According to Mr. Paley, every free response test is graded by 2 people, who independently grade the test, and if the score for any question differs by more than a point, they discuss the difference.

The Advanced Authentic Research (AAR) Program is a unique opportunity for students in grades 10-12. It is designed for students with interest, passion, curiosity, and perseverance to investigate an authentic topic of their choosing. Students are supported by a process-oriented curriculum developed by the AAR team and are encouraged to develop a mentorship with an industry expert. Students study families of functions including: linear, quadratic, polynomial, exponential, logarithmic, rational, and radical functions. title: Alternate schedule
text:
Gunn Wiki article: Alternate schedule

Alternate schedules are schedules that differ from the normal bell schedule and exist for a variety of reasons: most often to accommodate a long weekend, but sometimes also to accommodate standardized testing, teacher training, or other schoolwide events.  

Examples:
A full list of alternate schedules with dates and times can be found on Gunn's website. The following alternate schedules are reasonably common:

Friday off: Typically, if there is a long weekend with Friday off, then the Monday schedule is eliminated, Wednesday is moved to Monday, and Friday is moved to Wednesday. This means that PRIME is on Monday and SELF/Study Hall on Wednesday.
Monday off: If there is a long weekend with Monday off, then the 7-period Monday is simply eliminated.
Minimum day: Minimum days occur the Friday before Spring and Winter Break. They eliminate Lunch and SELF, and sometimes shorten the other classes.

title: Alternate schedule
text:

Late-Start mondays: Sometimes, there are late-start Mondays that run from 10:00 to 3:50. All classes are shortened to 35 minutes, Brunch is held from 10:00 to 10:15, and Lunch is held from 12:20 to 12:50, between periods 3 and 4.
Finals: During finals week, each period is extended to 2 hours, with periods 1 and 2 on one day; periods 3 and 4 on another; and 5, 6, and 7 on the last.
Extended lunch: When schoolwide events such as the Harvest Feast or Health Fair occur at lunch, the lunch period will sometimes be extended by 10 or 15 minutes (12:20-1:15, for example). The extra time is taken from the beginning of PRIME so all classes can remain a regular length of time; these events almost always happen on Wednesdays.

Structure:
Analysis H, like a typical PAUSD honors mathematics course, has a lot of homework, quizzes, and tests. Quizzes contribute to your grade about 1/3 as much as midterms, with homework making up 10% of the grade. This course is a problem-solving course; as such, the best way to excel in Analysis H is to do all the homework, review sheets, and old tests. If you do this work, you are much more likely to get an A in the course. Time in class is generally dedicated to introducing new material and doing practice problems, while the homework is generally used to practice the day's material, like a standard math class. There isn't much consistency to the topics taught in Analysis, as the course grabs topics from analytic geometry, discrete math, linear algebra, and calculus. text:
Gunn Wiki article: Bell

The bell is a device placed on many walls at Gunn that plays a 661 Hz sine wave tone for 4 seconds and follows the bell schedule, including alternate schedules. Timothy Herchen once recorded the bell.

The IPX clocks are capable of displaying a standby screen containing a date and a time; there is also code to only display the time, but it is not clear how this code is activated. When the clock boots, it first shows scrolling text reading "AtlasIED IPX IP-SDMF" and contains some information such as the firmware version (1.6.5), the MAC address, and the IP address. The MAC address of a speaker can also be found by reading a barcode label found under outdoor speakers or on the left face of indoor speakers. The text follows the format AtlasIED IPX IP-SDMF 1.6.5 AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF 0.0.0.0.

When the bell rings, scrolling text appears on the screen reading "Bell Schedules." This is likely the name of the event responsible for generating the bell tone.

The clocks do not scroll any text when a PA announcement is made or the fire alarm is activated.

text:

Installation of IPX clocks:
At the beginning of the 2022-2023 school year, the clocks were replaced with AtlasIED IPX IP-SDMF and IP-SDMF-72 speaker clocks. The 3 types of old clock-speaker hybrids were each replaced with different types of mounting hardware.

First round of installation:
The first clocks were installed in the summer of 2022 in the E building and the N building. These clocks were IP-SDMF-72 units in analog mode.

The N building clocks were installed by removing the analog clock and placing the slant enclosure where the clock previously was, routing the analog speaker wires into the new enclosure. The IP-SDMF-72 was then placed on top.

The E building clock installation was simpler; because the E building used compact clock-speaker combination units, it was sufficient to remove the old system and replace it with a slant enclosure.

Second round of installation:

title: Bell
text:
pact clock-speaker combination units, it was sufficient to remove the old system and replace it with a slant enclosure.

Second round of installation:
The remaining clocks were installed at the end of August 2022.

A similar process to the N building was followed to replace the remaining non-compact clock-speaker combination units, but normal IP-SDMF units were used instead of IP-SDMF-72 units. The clocks in the J building displayed the wrong time during the week of August 29, possibly as a result of the wires being connected incorrectly due to there being a different number of ports on the IP-SDMF from the IP-SDMF-72.

The compact clock-speaker combination units had the front panel removed and replaced with IP-SDMF units in flush mount enclosures. This allows the old Valcom enclosure to be reused, and the setup can still be easily maintained.

The digital Valcom IP clocks in the P building and S building were also replaced by IP-SDMF units in flush mount enclosures. This resulted in the new clocks looking similar to the old clocks.

Switching to the IP speaker:

title: Bell
text:
replaced by IP-SDMF units in flush mount enclosures. This resulted in the new clocks looking similar to the old clocks.

Switching to the IP speaker:
After the new clocks were installed, the IPX bell was enabled on September 9, playing a 1000 Hz sine wave tone for 4 seconds, which sounds like a softer version of the fire alarm. This was replaced with the 661 Hz sound on September 20.

Shutdowns and malfunctions:

title: Challenging courses
text:
Gunn Wiki article: Challenging courses

Under PAUSD policies, in order to fulfill course prerequisites without needing to take the course, students are entitled to challenge classes by examination.

According to BoardDocs,The challenge examination may be offered to requesting students when the course to be challenged is part of a sequence of courses normally taken in specific order, when the course to be challenged is normally required for entry into another course, or when a student’s previous/current experiences suggest appropriate mastery of course objectives.

During their enrollment in high school, students may challenge no more than two courses.  (BP 6146 - Courses of Study) (BP. 6146.1 - High School Graduation Requirements)
A student may challenge and attempt the competencies of a particular course only once. Failure to meet competency of a required course will result in a regular classroom enrollment.

title: Challenging courses
text:
empt the competencies of a particular course only once. Failure to meet competency of a required course will result in a regular classroom enrollment.
A student may not challenge a course in which the student has previously received a failing grade, a course previously taken where credit was received, a course more elementary than a course in which credit has previously been earned, an Honors course, an Advanced Placement course, living skills, or a physical education course.
A student may challenge only one course per semester. This may be a course in which the student is enrolled or any other approved course offering. A student may not attempt credit for a course below the student’s ability or grade placement.

Tier 1:
Tier 1 clubs are the lowest tier. They do not receive any funding and are technically not allowed to raise or own money, though of course money for supplies can be informally raised. Tier 1 is the only tier that is not required to submit monthly meeting "minutes" to document their actions. Tier 1 clubs are typically more informal and don't go through many technicalities. An example of this tier is Card Game Club.

Tier 2:
Tier 2 clubs are allowed to spend and raise money as well as organize events. They must submit meeting minutes monthly to track their decisions. Some examples are TEDxGunnHighSchool and GSA. 

Tier 3:
Tier 3 clubs can, in addition to spend/raise money and hold events, have field trips. They are typically larger and more prestigious clubs, like the Debate Club, Math Circle, and Thespian Club.

Running a club:
To keep their charter, a club will need to:

Clubs in practice:
An ideal club as described by the SEC is quite different for a club in practice.

Firstly, many Tier 1 clubs would be better characterized as "cliques" instead of clubs, consisting of a close group for friends and a "warm body" club advisor rather than just a bunch of like-minded folk with an enthusiastic advisor. Such clubs are often created by friend groups trying to pad their college applications by becoming some club officers; consequently, they often die out soon after the members of the group graduate. Even so, not all Tier 1 clubs follow this path. As Tier 1 clubs are easier to charter and have less restrictions (for example, meeting minutes aren't required for all meetings and secretary and treasurer positions can be combined), being a Tier 1 club is the best option for many newer general interest clubs without tons of members and thus, don't require school funding and events.

title: Clubs
text:
g a Tier 1 club is the best option for many newer general interest clubs without tons of members and thus, don't require school funding and events.  

Second, the Club Constitution for Tier 1 clubs serves mainly as a ceremonial document. Many Tier 1 clubs use no formal process to make decisions since the members may already be friends, and are capable of working things out by themselves without a constitution to dictate how they should act. Although the SEC stipulates that the constitution should guide how a club is run, this is impossible to enforce.

Third, in the same vein, attendance is loosely enforced. In the past, even clubs significantly underpopulated in the fall were often allowed to continue their activities in the spring. As of 2024-2025, SEC technically enforces club attendance, but gives underpopulated clubs a "warning" halfway through the semester that the must meet the 10-member quota for the rest of the semester.

Finally, it is less important to keep attendance up during the spring semester because failure to do so only disqualifies the club for fast-track re-chartering for the following fall; they can still re-charter normally. 

Club government:
Jacob Chiu posits the following principles for club government:

A club is made for the benefit of its members, and, more generally, the student body. If a club cannot operate in such a way that it fulfills that purpose, it ought to be disbanded. As such, a club should avoid having the will of the SEC, school administrators, and students trying to harm the club forcibly imposed upon it.
The job of a club government is to ensure the club runs smoothly. Governmental functions should not interfere significantly with the normal activities of the club.

title: Clubs
text:
lub government is to ensure the club runs smoothly. Governmental functions should not interfere significantly with the normal activities of the club. 
There are three sorts of decision-making processes: 1) informal consensus, in which all members/officers come to an agreement or compromise on decisions; 2) rules-based, in which clearly defined rules dictate how the club operates or how decisions are to be made; and 3) deadlock, when members are unable to come to a consensus and no decisions can be made. Informal consensus is better than rules because it is more adaptable, and often, more efficient. However, if a club grows too big, its members/officers aren't friendly, or a very important/controversial issue is being decided, this can lead to deadlock if there aren't clearly written rules to keep things moving. The purpose of a Club Constitution is to leave as much flexibility for the current officers while avoiding deadlock. For example, a Constitution should usually lay out how to elect and impeach club officers because those are highly contentious issues.

title: Credit
text:
Gunn Wiki article: Credit

Credit is what is earned by passing a course. Semester-long courses result in 5 credits, and year-long courses result in 10 credits.

Repeating classes:
Courses may only be repeated if the student earned a D or F, or it is a repeatable course. Credit will not be earned a second time if a D was earned, but it will be earned for the first time if an F was earned. The individual GPA point also gets replaced by the new one.

In addition, getting a D or F may result in automatic summer school enrollment, which removes the need to repeat a course during the school year.

In the case of repeatable courses, they can always be repeated, and repeating results in more credit than taking it once. The GPA score is not replaced in this case.

According to Mr. Olah, the new system has two functions: teachers can optionally use it to take attendance, and students are required to use it whenever they leave class. title: Evidence-Based Grading
text:
Gunn Wiki article: Evidence-Based Grading

Evidence-based grading, or Standards-based grading was a new grading system introduced in the 2024-25 school year aiming to take the focus off counting points and shift students' focus to learning, mastery, and growth in a subject. It is planned to be rolled out to all classes over the next few years.

Mechanics:
Under this system, for each test taken, students are given a score of 4, 3, 2, 1, or No Mark in each of several skill areas. A score of 4 represents a skill level exceeding understanding, while 3 is showing understanding, 2 is approaching understanding, and 1 is developing understanding.

At the end of each semester, the test scores in each skill area are composited into a single score based upon a recency-biased mode. That is to say, the final score in a skill area is given by the score that appeared the most often, with a bias towards recent scores. Then, a letter grade is assigned based on the combination of skill area scores. Exact details differ between teachers, but in general it works like this:

title: Evidence-Based Grading
text:
a letter grade is assigned based on the combination of skill area scores. Exact details differ between teachers, but in general it works like this: 

scores of 3 and 4 are treated as more or less equivalent, and getting 3s and 4s in every category gets the student an A.  
one 2 in any category gets a B,  
multiple 2's generally gets a C 
one 1 generally gets a D 
multiple 1's gets an F/NM. 

Additionally, evidence-based grading systems tend to focus less on homework and also allow for test retakes as a logical method of determining students' academic mastery without being held to a rigid timetable and reduce student stress.

Benefits and Drawbacks:

title: Evidence-Based Grading
text:
a logical method of determining students' academic mastery without being held to a rigid timetable and reduce student stress.

Benefits and Drawbacks:
As stated earlier, the system is intended to better gauge students' learning and improvement over the semester. It also attempts to discourage desperately seeking points rather than learning itself, though the fact that numerical scores determine their final grade by a mathematical formula still leads to students seeking constantly to jump the barrier from one score to another. Also, the system is somewhat less concrete than the traditional points-based system, leading to a certain ambiguity over what scores a student deserves, though in theory this is offset by the holistic process used to determine final letter grades. It is certainly as of this time new to teachers, who are having some trouble adjusting.

title: Evidence-Based Grading
text:
e holistic process used to determine final letter grades. It is certainly as of this time new to teachers, who are having some trouble adjusting.    

Anecdotally, it appears that EBG grading is leading to an overall grade deflation, with more people getting B's and C's and fewer people getting A's. However, this is expected to change over the course of the semester as people master the skills in the course and start doing retakes, if the system works as intended. This grade deflation still stresses out students though, as they are used to getting A's and B's. Furthermore, one student has complained that the school from which Gunn's EBG system is modelled, Adlai Stevenson High School in Illinois, has much better support for students seeking to improve their grades.   

Classes using Evidence-Based Grading:
According to an email sent to parents by the principal, only the following classes have fully implemented evidence-based grading:

Chemistry and AP Chemistry [what about Chemistry H?]
Conceptual Physics, Physics, AP Physics 1 and AP Physics C.
AP English Literature
Algebra 1

Conceptual Physics, Physics, AP Physics 1 and AP Physics C.
AP English Literature
Algebra 1
AP Computer Science Principles

However, the following classes have also been implementing some parts of it:
AP US History -- Tests are corrected instead of being retaken; projects can be revised
American Classics H -- with Hernandez, Halter, Weymouth, and possibly others. Retake policy is unclear at this time. Class work is counted in the grade as one of the assignments.
AP Calculus BC used an evidence-based grading system (but with no test retakes and homework as a percentage of the grade) in the 2024-2025 school year, but due to its labor-intensiveness and minimal benefits it will not be continued. 

Popular Opinion of EBG:
Of students:

title: Evidence-Based Grading
text:
in the 2024-2025 school year, but due to its labor-intensiveness and minimal benefits it will not be continued. 

Popular Opinion of EBG:
Of students:
Many students oppose evidence-based grading due to it causing grade deflation. An Oracle survey reported in December 2024 that around half of students thought EBG was either "very ineffective" or "ineffective", with one-quarter saying it was "neither" and one-quarter "effective" or "very effective".   

Of parents:
A Signal group chat on the topic of evidence-based grading attracted over 250 parents, most of whom were parents of juniors and seniors and opposed to evidence-based grading. 

Of teachers:
Teachers appear to have a mixed impression of evidence-based grading, with some teachers advocating for it and some teachers disliking it. Currently, there appears to be no consensus among teachers on its utility.

text:

One teacher who has voiced her support for EBG is Ms. Pennington, who has used the system for the last few years. In a letter to The Oracle, she writes that the system rewards learning even though it may deflate grades for students who use the methods common to traditional grading to "game the system" and get high grades without real learning and growth. Ms. Zizmor has also expressed support for EBG grading, and has used it in her Chemistry classes for a few years.

Anecdotally, Ms. Merchant and Ms. Tantod have expressed opposition to standards-based grading. In particular, Ms. Tantod said that the Analysis H teachers planned to use traditional grading for as long as possible.

Biology teachers have also expressed opposition to EBG because the recency-biased system does not apply so well to the very different units of Bio.

title: Fire alarm
text:
Gunn Wiki article: Fire alarm

The fire alarm has frequently gone off at Gunn High School for the past few years. Usually, the causes of these alarms are unknown, but some conjectured causes are students who want to skip class, vaping, Chem experiments that go wrong, cooking smoke, or crows. The cause of these alarms is almost never a fire though, which defeats the purpose of the alarms. Most recently, three fire alarms went off on August 19, August 21, and August 22, 2024. The school district is currently attempting to fix the fire alarm system  so that the fire alarms only go off if there is an actual fire, and do not go off for unknown reasons, unnecessarily wasting class time. 

In the 2022–2023 school year, the traditional loud, disruptive fire alarms were replaced with a calm voice coming from the new clocks telling students to evacuate with the wall-mounted flashers still operating as a visual cue. In 2023–2024, the auditory warning was replaced with short, calm beeps coming from the clock.

title: FlexTime
text:
Gunn Wiki article: FlexTime

FlexTime was a period created to not be behind the instructional minute requirements after transitioning to a block schedule with less instructional time per class per week (232 -> 225 minutes). For this to be considered instructional time, students must be required to attend some class during FlexTime, but because they can check in with any teacher, there needs to be a new system, as InfiniteCampus does not support this. Because of this, a new web app, called the FlexTime App, allowed teachers to mark students present with them and reserve appointments.

It was succeeded in the 2020-2021 school year by Gunn Together.

Student reactions:
Students often try to escape campus during Flex because they believe is useless, and often get away with it.

Not to be confused with FlexTime, the period that this app tracks.

The FlexTime App was a web app that teachers use to say that a student is with them during FlexTime. (FlexTime no longer exists at Gunn.) 

Students can reserve appointments in this app, as well as view their check-ins, and teachers can check students in by scanning their ID card or giving their 950 number. It can be found at https://tutorial-gunn.pausd.org, although both the student and the teacher portals have been taken down.

title: FlexiSched
text:
Gunn Wiki article: FlexiSched

FlexiSched (Pronounds FLEXie-skedge) is the application used to schedule PRIME and Study Hall appointments with teachers. Appointments open on Mondays and closes at the end of 7th period on Wednesdays. 

FlexiSched is also used by teachers to take attendance, though (at least in the past) the school doesn't appear to check this. There is a story of a student who skipped PRIME all year and suffered no consequences.  

How to use:
FlexiSched can be accessed at https://gunn.flexisched.net, which will prompt you to sign in using either ClassLink or Google. This takes you to a dashboard that displays your current PRIME/Study Hall schedule, with a pencil icon to the right that allows you to edit it. The dropdown menu on the top bar allows you to access a list of PRIME appointments and your attendance.

title: Freshman

Gunn Wiki article: Freshman

A freshman, frosh, or 9th grader is a student in their first year of high school after graduating from a middle school. The color yellow is typically associated with freshmen during school-wide inter-grade events like Homecoming.

Course selection:
Freshmen are required to have 7 classes, 5 of which are in fixed disciplines.

English:
Freshmen can take English 9 or English 9A.

Social Studies:
All freshmen take World History (or World History SLC). Starting in the 2025-2026 school year, all freshmen will be required to take a new California Ethnic Studies course, per California law. The World History course will be shortened to one semester.

Math:
Students who took Math 8 take Algebra 1 in 9th grade. Students who took Algebra 8 have a choice between Geometry  and Geometry H. Freshman who skipped a year of math and did Geometry H in 8th grade take Algebra 2 + Trig H.

Science:
Freshmen have the choice between Biology or Biology H.

PE:
Freshmen must take either PE 9 or Zero period PE 9. PE electives may not be taken during the freshman year.

title: GPA
text:
Gunn Wiki article: GPA

A GPA (grade point average) is a number that attempts to summarize a student's academic performance. It is defined as the mean of the grade point scores of every class.

Grade point scores:
Grade point scores can be found from a letter grade. If a score is "null," then the class is not counted toward the GPA.

Gunn reports +/- grading for most classes; however, the +/- grading is not factored into the GPA.

Weighted GPA:
Certain classes, generally AP and honors classes, are considered "weighted" and may not be taken by freshmen due to UC requirements. For each of these classes, the individual grade point score is increased by 1, for a maximum of 5.

This caused some controversy due to some students not having this benefit until their senior year, which resulted in the GPA concept being split into an unweighted GPA (uwGPA), without the score increases, and the weighted GPA (wGPA), where the score boosts are present.

Geometry A was previously an advanced-lane course offered to students coming from 8th grade Algebra or Algebra 1. However, it was discontinued in the 2023-2024 school year due to de-laning efforts. 

Prior to discontinuation:
Students taking Algebra 8 in middle school could choose either Geometry H or Geometry A, while students taking 9th grade Algebra 1 could only choose Geometry or Geometry A. Geometry A students would by default continue through the Advanced lane, taking Algebra 2/Trig A, IAC, and AP Calculus AB (if applicable).

All Algebra students can now choose either Geometry or Geometry H. The Honors lane remains unchanged, but students in Geometry now elect whether to take Algebra 2 or Algebra 2/Trig A, in effect pushing back the lane split by one year.

Course Catalog Description:
This is a hands-on course that will provide students real-life experience in mechanical design, machine shop skills, engineering project work and leadership. The curriculum is designed to fit the needs of both four-year-college-bound students and those interested in a two-year career tech education. Conceptual instruction begins with the design cycle, which students experience in all stages, including hands-on skill development from brainstorming to prototyping to manufacturing and testing. Mechanism design and prototyping, programming, electronics, pneumatics, machining and welding, and CAD (computer-aided design) technologies are introduced to all students using industry-standard equipment. Applications of scientific and engineering principles, group dynamics, leadership and communication skills are developed in an activity-oriented approach including informal classroom challenges and two or more FIRST Robotics competitions each

An application process will be used to award spaces within GRT based on skills necessary for team success, and detailed information regarding this process will be published in January. Students who have completed Introduction to Engineering Design, Principles of Engineering and Robotics, an Automotive Technology course, or a Stage Technology course will be given special consideration during the selection process.

title: Gunn Student Simulator
text:
Gunn Wiki article: Gunn Student Simulator

Gunn Student Simulator is a simple text based game, hosted on Github here. It satirizes the student workload at Gunn, giving you more and more work per night to manage until you have no time for sleep nor friends. It also satirizes SELF, using the juxtaposition of cheery school assemblies with the almost comedic amount of work assigned, characterizing SELF as a useless distraction instead of an actual fix. 

The "Info" tab on the website shows the following text: This game accurately portrays the life of a Gunn student. Students at Gunn must balance their social lives, academics, careers, and commitment to SELF, but to balance one would unbalance another. To win, you need to be able to take the SAT/ACT early so that you can graduate early. However, you can only do that in your free time since homework and test studying takes priority. Anyone may (and should) make own version of this game, though please consider crediting the creator or link to this game somewhere. 

Gameplay:

title: Gunn Student Simulator
text:
ority. Anyone may (and should) make own version of this game, though please consider crediting the creator or link to this game somewhere. 

Gameplay:
The player starts by studying for the SAT/ACT; each time the option is clicked they become 2% more ready. With each passing day they receive homework assignments and tests to study for; as they do this they gradually lose their readiness for the SAT/ACT. If they do not complete their homework or study adequately for tests their grades drop, which will result in their parents disowning them (losing the game). There are also other time-consuming obstacles like after-school SELF and hanging out with friends. Repercussions that will also eventually lead to losing are suffered if they opt out of these things, but if they do them they lose valuable time to study.

title: Gunnels
text:
Gunn Wiki article: Gunnels

The Gunnels, or Gunn Tunnels, are a pair of culverts forming the Barron Creek Bypass Structure. They are walkable during the dry season and have for years been a popular location for Gunn students to "hang out". They are relatively well-known in the community surrounding Palo Alto, so students from other schools often visit as well. Graffiti covers most of the tunnel walls and large parts of the floors. As of Autumn 2024, there is still a soiled sofa in the tunnel. The Gunnels have a relatively low clearance and are only adequately ventilated near storm drains. Due to their construction and notoriety, the Gunnels are a wonderful venue for echo sax and other acoustic performances.

The tunnels are visible on OpenStreetMap but not Google Maps. You can view them at this link.

Barron Creek:
Barron Creek begins in the foothills and runs north, meeting Gunn High School. From there it enters a debris basin (a basin to capture debris and prevent it from going downstream) and flows through a pipe under Los Robles Avenue, emerging at El Camino. It continues north until it empties, along with Adobe Creek into the Palo Alto Flood Basin. The flood basin is connected to the San Francisco Bay through a tide gate, which allows water to flow out, but not into the flood basin, ensuring its water levels remain low to prevent flooding.

title: Gunnels
text:
isco Bay through a tide gate, which allows water to flow out, but not into the flood basin, ensuring its water levels remain low to prevent flooding.

To resolve the problem of frequent flooding during winter storms, the Gunnels (officially known as the Barron Creek Bypass) were constructed to divert water to Matadero Creek in times of heavy rain. The bypass (now called the Matadero Bypass) continues past Matadero Creek, meets the Stanford Channel (an artificial channel which brings water from Santa Rita Creek) at Matadero Avenue, and reunites with Matadero Creek at El Camino Real. Gunn students most often visit the section from the flood basin to Matadero Creek. 

Entrances:
The two main entrances to the Gunnels used by students are at the debris basin and at Matadero Creek, just beyond the Barron Park Donkeys. Both are sealed by a grate which has been pried open.

text:

According to Gunn rules, all students in the hallways during class time must hold a hall pass. 

A hall pass is a laminated red tag, about the size of a half-sheet of paper, that is hung on a lanyard. Each classroom is given 2 hall passes with their classroom number written on them. Starting 2025-2026, the hall pass system will be digitized.

title: Homecoming
text:
Gunn Wiki article: Homecoming

Homecoming is a yearly school tradition, typically held in the Fall, in which the classes compete against each other. Alumni return for events like the Night Rally and football game.

Homecoming is one week long, with activities beginning before school on Monday, and culminating in the homecoming football game held at Gunn on Friday. There is also a homecoming dance on Saturday.

Daily activities:
Each day of the week, the four classes have their own dress-up themes, and are judged daily in a competition. There are games held at brunch (like Stuff-a-bench), and Lunch (like Shooting Stars).

Night Rally:
On Thursday night, the Night Rally is held in Titan Gym. Among other activities of the night, each class competes in performing their own Airbands dance, which is judged by alumni.

Football Game:
On Friday night, there is a football game played at the track against another school. This is usually one of the first games of the football season.

Key facts: department: sciencew; title: Human Anatomy and Physiology; length: year; weighted: no

Human Anatomy is a science elective course with a light homework load. 

Course Catalog Description:
This college-prep course covers the design structure of the human body and how it meets the demands of everyday living. Students explore connections between form and function through units in cell biology that include, histology (tissue study), and the following body systems: Integumentary, Nervous, Skeletal, Muscular, Respiratory, Cardiovascular, Immune, Renal, and Digestive. Students will investigate the integration of these systems in the context of homeostasis.

title: Human Anatomy and Physiology
text:
Respiratory, Cardiovascular, Immune, Renal, and Digestive. Students will investigate the integration of these systems in the context of homeostasis.

This course includes lecture, discussion, and significant practical experience while working with microscopes, anatomical models, laboratory investigations, and various dissections. Human A&P emphasizes the structural organization of the body, identification of anatomical parts, and the coordination of systems as a foundation for understanding health, disease, and medical practice.

Prerequisite(s): Successful completion of a biology course (for graduation requirement) and a physical science course (Chemistry strongly recommended)

A junior is an 11th grader. Junior year is generally considered to be the most stressful year at Gunn, as most people take their hardest classes, extracurriculars, and standardized tests such as the SAT or ACT this year. 

Course selection:
English:
Juniors can take a semester of American Literature or American Classics H in even years, and a semester of World Literature or World Classics H in odd years. They also choose an English elective from a wide variety of options such as Visual Story, Analytic Writing, and Comp. Lit + Film.

Social Studies:
Juniors can choose to either take AP US History or a semester of US History and a social studies elective. Most juniors choose to take AP US History because they want to increase their course rigor or because they are genuinely interested in history; some juniors, however, choose to take US History as they want to avoid the high levels of work required to succeed in AP US History.

Juniors who took Geometry or Geometry H the previous year have a choice between Algebra 2, Algebra 2/Trig A, and Algebra 2/Trig H. Students who took Algebra 2 + Trig A generally move on to IAC. title: Knives

In accordance with the California Education Code, PAUSD policies ban weapons of any sort. 

California rules:
California's Education Code bans all "injurious objects" from schools, which include BB guns, firearms, various other weapons defined here, machine guns, switchblades, and tear gas. It also imposes a blanket ban on any "objects capable of inflicting substantial bodily damage, not necessary for the academic purpose of the pupil."

In practice:
School administrators have clarified that pocket-knives are definitely not allowed at school; this seems to fit the California definition of an object capable of being very dangerous, which is not associated with academics. Straightedges, scissors, etc. are probably not included in this definition, and it is unlikely that an administrator would suspend a student for possessing a butter-knife -- though they may confiscate it since it is technically a "knife".

title: Little Theater

Gunn Wiki article: Little Theater

Little Theater is a theatre at Henry M. Gunn High School. It is located in the same building on the opposite side of the wall to Spangenberg Theater, and is where all Theatre (and occasionally Dramatic Literature) classes are held. It is also where smaller productions are held, including theatre finals. Looking at the stage, the door to the left leads to the Green Room, while the right hand door leads to a workshop for Stage Tech's construction and paint crews. Both have further doors leading up to the attic area above the Little Theater, colloquially called "Purgatory" for it's complete lack of lighting (requiring headlamps to be worn while working in the area). Both the Green Room and workshop have massive garage-style doors alongside regular doors to access Spangenberg's stage, though only the garage door to the workshop is regularly opened for various construction activities.

Gunn Wiki article: M-1

M-1 is the classroom for the photography classes: Photo 1, Advanced Photography, Advanced Photography H, and AP Photography. It consists of a series of connected rooms, the biggest being the main classroom and the main darkroom. These two rooms are connected by a short hallway which has other very small rooms (three of which are not big enough to comfortably fit more than 3 people), which are used for various purposes. There is also a lockable storage room for cameras. Ms. Durquet and Mr. Gleason are the teachers who used M-1 in the 2024-2025 school year. 

Main classroom:
Part of the M building, between L and N near the Miranda Road side of campus. The floor is not made of the same linoleum material or carpet as some other classrooms are, and is instead concrete. The room contains a few desktop computers which are connected to scanners (for film photos or negatives) and can run Photoshop.

Arguably a part of the main classroom is the camera closet, which is locked when not in use. It contains cameras and camera equipment such as bags.

Darkrooms:

title: M-1
text:
a part of the main classroom is the camera closet, which is locked when not in use. It contains cameras and camera equipment such as bags.

Darkrooms:
The main M-1 classroom connects to a professional darkroom of the same size as the classroom. It houses 14 enlargers for printing film photos, materials for printing like photo paper and darkroom chemicals, a very large sink used as a table for paper development, and  storage for used chemicals before disposal. It has normal overhead lights and dim red safety lights for when the darkroom is in use.

The hallway connecting the main classroom to the darkroom has a few small rooms along it. The largest of these is a "wet room" containing a large sink, materials for mixing darkroom chemicals, racks to dry printed photos, et cetera. The other rooms are tiny, barely big enough for 3 people, and are mostly used as storage and complete-darkness rooms for handling undeveloped film. One of them is used as a "kitchen" for tea-brewing and such; all four of these rooms have sinks.

Course Catalog Description:
Marine Biology is a second-year biology college-prep course that builds upon and extends biological, chemical, and physical processes developed during the first two years of science courses. Students will take an in-depth look at the features of the ocean and the variety of plant and animal life that lives within. They will investigate how life in the ocean is interconnected and the impact that humans have on that system. Topics will be developed through laboratory exercises, discussions, lectures, demonstrations, informational research projects, and field trips. Please note, this is a laboratory science class where scientific skills and methods (including data analysis and laboratory write-ups) will be emphasized.

title: Math
text:
Gunn Wiki article: Math

Math is a department with a variety of classes, most of which have a clear intended order. 30 credits are required for graduation, in addition to passing Algebra 2 or an equivalent class. The current math department head is Mr. Hahn.

Pathways:
Students who took Algebra 8 in 8th grade may choose between Geometry A and Geometry H for 9th grade. Students who took Geometry H in 8th grade after skipping in middle school generally enter Algebra 2 + Trig H, although some people drop to Algebra 2 + Trig A or even repeat Geometry H if they did not do well in the course. 

In previous years, students who took Math 8 in 8th grade took Algebra 1 in 9th grade, then having a choice between Geometry and Geometry A the next year, however, they could also take Geometry A during Summer School to directly go to Algebra 2 + Trig A the next year. 

From here, students generally stay in the same lane, although there are instances of lane changes, such as changing from Analysis to IAC.

title: Math
text:

From here, students generally stay in the same lane, although there are instances of lane changes, such as changing from Analysis to IAC.

Students who take IAC then do AP Calculus AB the next year if they wish to get a fourth year of math. Precalculus students may also do this, although it is less common, as taking Precalc before senior year requires a lane change. Analysis students have the choice between AP Calculus AB and AP Calculus BC. Students who skipped in middle school and thus take Calculus BC in their junior year can choose to do a math elective such as AP Statistics or take an MVC, Lin Alg, or Diff Eq Class at Foothill College. These courses do not currently accept dual credit, but their credit will be accepted by colleges.

Skipping classes:
The district has made it very difficult to skip courses. Students typically take a placement course before entering middle school that puts them in either in the normal (Algebra in 8th grade) or accelerated (Geometry H in 8th grade) track.

There is sparse use of Schoology; many teachers instead use a shared Google folder.
Homework is checked for completion

By his own account, he had a similar upbringing and academic background to most Gunn students (which cannot be said of the majority of teachers), so he is generally understanding about kids' stressors, displaying a genuine interest in what's going on in their lives. He also rarely gets mad at students, even when they are on their phones during class or forget to turn in homework; instead he gently tells them to stop.

She has strict rules about how notebooks are to be kept, mainly to make it easier for her to grade them. For example, she insists that complete their work in pen for readability purposes; except for diagrams, drawings, and math where constantly crossing out mistakes would instead impede readability. Assignments are to be logged in a table of contents with the date and first page indicated. (Multi-page assignments are assumed to be continued on the next page, unless a note saying "continued on page __" is at the bottom of a page.) According to her, she does not often grant extensions because students tend to procrastinate away the extra time given. However, she does allow assignment revisions.

title: Office hours
text:
Gunn Wiki article: Office hours

Office hours can either refer to the various Zoom meetings teachers allocated for students to come to to seek help when COVID-19 first started, or the Tutorial period that happened after school during the 2020-2021 school year.  

It no longer exists, though students can meet with teachers during PRIME.   

Spring of 2020:
Office hours were originally created during Phase 2 of school closure because many connections between students and teachers dropped, and students often found distance learning difficult. When Phase 3 started, teachers were still not allowed to require synchronous time, because some students may be busy during the time teachers decide on synchronous time. Of these, Hoover and Ohlone are choice schools, which means that any student can enter a lottery to go there regardless of where in Palo Alto they live. Hoover is more academically focused while Ohlone offers a somewhat more open, holistic learning experience and has a farm.

Middle Schools:
There are three middle schools: Fletcher, Greene, and Jane Lathrop Stanford (JLS). Fletcher and Greene were formerly named Terman and Jordan respectively, but their names were changed in the 2018 – 2019 school year due to the namesakes' involvement in eugenics. Of the three schools, JLS is the largest. Its graduating students are split between Gunn and Paly, while all Fletcher students go to Gunn and all Greene students go to Paly. 

High Schools:
The two comprehensive high schools in the district are Gunn High School and Palo Alto High School. They are rivals. There is also a third high school, Palo Alto Middle College High School, but it is a special school that has a limited enrollment of about 150-200 students and allows students to take Foothill College classes on-campus.

PRIME (short for Personal Reteaching Intervention Mentorship Enrichment) is a mandatory study-hall/office-hours period following 7th period on Wednesdays. Students are assigned by default to a PRIME teacher but may schedule an appointment with another teacher on FlexiSched.

PRIME is the successor to Gunn Together, though with more emphasis on Flex (the predecessor of Gunn Together)-like periods.

Students have complained that PRIME is pointless and that they should be allowed to go home if they don't need to visit teachers. Another criticism stems from the bureaucratic nature of needing to sign up for PRIME teachers on FlexiSched rather than having the flexibility of visiting whatever teacher(s) one wants.

Students with 7th period preps must still attend PRIME.
All students will be assigned to a PRIME classroom with one of their teachers on their schedule and will report at the beginning of prime to that teacher.

students will be assigned to a PRIME classroom with one of their teachers on their schedule and will report at the beginning of prime to that teacher.

Some teachers, commonly PE teachers, turn a blind eye to students skipping PRIME, so you can just sign up for their PRIME, stay until they take attendance and mark you present, then leave.

title: Prep
text:
Gunn Wiki article: Prep

Key facts: department: other; length: sem; credit: no

A Prep period is a period where no class is being taken, for both students and teachers. It generally does not refer to zero period and period 8 when they are not being taken.

Obtaining a prep:
There are 5 ways to obtain a prep:

Taking classes outside the 1-7 range:
By registering for a course during zero period or period 8, a prep is automatically placed during periods 1-7 for the duration of that course. Additionally, each semester in Kick-start results in a single-semester prep during the following school year.

Athletics:
Students who participate in athletics do not need to attend PE, provided that they fill out the proper forms. This is not a full prep, as they must return to PE the day after their final game.

Signing up for the "Prep" course:
Students may also take fewer than 7 classes by explicitly requesting the course called "Prep." Each grade has its own minimum number of classes, which excludes preps.

Not signing up for 7 year-long classes:

title: Prep
text:
requesting the course called "Prep." Each grade has its own minimum number of classes, which excludes preps.

Not signing up for 7 year-long classes:
Students can sign up for less than 7 year-long classes, especially as an upperclassmen. Some may choose to have a prep the entire school year by not filling up all your block periods with classes, and some may choose to have a semester long prep by taking a semester-long class during a period in one semester but then not taking another semester-long course in the other semester.

Dropping a class:
Even when you have a packed schedule, you can still change it in the middle of the school year by dropping the class you're struggling the most in/have the least interest in.

Should I sign up for this course?:
Take a prep if your schedule is already burdened with multiple AP and honors classes, or if you have sports or other extracurricular commitments (e.g. Robotics). It will be a lifesaver for you. If you are interested in being a teaching assistant, a prep also allows you to work with the teacher you're TA-ing for more flexibly.

Gunn Wiki article: School chromebooks

Every Gunn student is provided with an Acer 512 Flip Chromebook. 
Details:
The computers come with Gorilla Glass touchscreens and feature a 180-degree hinge that can convert the computer into a tablet, disabling the keyboard. Since a magnetic sensor is used to detect the flipped lid, placing a normally opened one on top of a closed one causes it to enter tablet mode, collapsing all browser tabs. 

Chromebooks have two cameras: one at the top of the screen, where most laptop webcams are found. The other is at the back of the keyboard, which is designed to be used while the computer is in tablet mode. 

Chromebooks can charge from two USB-C ports, one on each side of the computer. Also, they have a USB 3.0 port, a micro SD slot, and an audio jack on the left side. There is another USB 3.0 port on the right side. The power button is located on the left, while a volume adjustment is present on the right.

title: School year
text:
Gunn Wiki article: School year

A school year, as opposed to a calendar year, describes the length of time that students are in a given grade. The school year is subdivided into two grading periods called semesters, which are for convenience subdivided into two quarters each. The current school year is the 2025-2026 school year. 

Within the school year are four notable breaks: 

Thanksgiving break, occurring in late November, lasts 1 week.
Winter Break, in late December and early January, lasts 2 weeks. It divides the first and second semesters.
Spring Break, in early April, lasts 1 week.
Summer Break, beginning in early June and ending in mid-August, lasts 2½ months.

title: Schoology
text:
Gunn Wiki article: Schoology

Schoology is the platform where PAUSD middle- and high-schoolers receive and submit their assignments. Grades are also usually posted there, as are course updates from teachers to their classes. There is the ability for students to personally message teachers on Schoology, though many teachers dislike being messaged in this way. 

Features:
Schoology has a number of features that enhance its utility:

digital quizzes and tests
discussion boards
support for Google Docs as assignments
EdPuzzles
PDFs and Word documents
a digital calendar
a "resources" section that allows you to store files as well as submit assignments from Google Drive, Dropbox, Youtube and Vimeo

"Wellness not Grades":
At 4:17 pm on August 25, 2021, the grades menu mysteriously disappeared in all of PAUSD. The purpose was unknown, but the "Mastery" feature still exists. Rumors on the Gunn Discord claimed this was to improve the "mental health" of students, but it is more likely simply because PAUSD wants to entirely switch to mastery-based grades. Grades have since been restored.

title: Schoology
text:
al health" of students, but it is more likely simply because PAUSD wants to entirely switch to mastery-based grades. Grades have since been restored.

Schoology Plus:
Schoology Plus is a web extension that added various features to Schoology, notably "what-if grades" that allow students to enter a hypothetical grade on an assignment and see how it affects their overall grade. It was banned from school chromebooks at the request of Mr. Kaneko, who cited web security reasons, at the annoyance of many students. However, it can still be used on personal laptops. 

Opinion by teachers:
Teachers' opinions on Schoology are widely varied, though outright praise for the application is rarely heard. Many teachers dislike Schoology for a variety of reasons, for example, the Schoology messaging function is clunky and it is impossible to search for past messages. Usage of Schoology is similarly varied, with some teachers using it extensively to complete almost all assignments digitally, while others only use it to post grades at regular intervals in compliance with district regulations.

title: Science
text:
Gunn Wiki article: Science

The Science Department is the department at Gunn that handles all the science classes. Specific subjects covered include Biology, Chemistry, Physics, and Environmental Sciences. 

Progression:
All freshmen are required to take a biology course, either Biology or Biology H. Sophomores take a Physical Science course, typically Chemistry or Chemistry H. Juniors and seniors are not required to take a science course, though they are recommended to. 

Idiosyncrasies:
Science teachers typically have some sort of notebook policy, though it's not always enforced.
Lecture slides are typically not posted.
Homework is not checked, though pre-labs are. 
Tests are locked in the classroom and it is made extremely clear to students that they are not to photograph, record, or remove their tests from the classroom.
Courses are not typically standardized between teachers of the same class, unlike in the Math department. 

See Also:

text:
Gunn Wiki article: Science Olympiad

Key facts: tier: 2; advisor: Ms. Pennington; room: L1; frequency: weekly; meeting day: thursday; time: lunch

Science Olympiad is a club that is known for sending a group of 30 people to represent Gunn at Science Olympiad tournaments. It was founded in the 2005-2006 school year. The club meets on Thursdays in L-1, with Ms. Pennington being the longterm advisor of the club. There are usually fun science trivia games being hosted in the club, and the club also meets outside of school to prepare for Science Olympiad tournaments.

title: Semester
text:
Gunn Wiki article: Semester

A Semester is half of a school year. The first semester begins in mid-August and ends in late December, while the second semester begins in early January and ends in early June. Students are given a grade on their transcript for each semester. 

Although most courses last for the whole year, some, notably English elective courses, only last for a semester. Of the year-long courses, a few, like AP Physics C and AP Computer Science A, teach materially different content between the two semesters, but this is not common.

Senioritis is a common affliction of Seniors during the second semester and is characterized by a lack of motivation to continue with one's studies.

title: Senior
text:
Gunn Wiki article: Senior

Seniors are students in 12th grade. 

Courses:
Seniors generally have more flexibility in course selection, having likely fulfilled most of their graduation requirements. Seniors are required to enroll in a minimum of 5 courses. 

Social Studies:
Seniors are required to take two semesters of Social Studies, one of which must be in Economics. In practice this means that people either take Economics and a Social Studies elective, or AP Micro- and Macroeconomics. There is talk of requiring some financial literacy class in the future. 

English:
Seniors are required to take 2 semesters of English. They may either take American Classics/World Literature and an elective (similar to Juniors), or 2 semesters of AP English Literature. 

Science:
Seniors are not required to take any science course, since all graduation requirements are fulfilled by taking Biology in 9th grade and a physical science in 10th grade. Many Seniors do choose to take Science classes. 

Math:

title: Senior
text:
equirements are fulfilled by taking Biology in 9th grade and a physical science in 10th grade. Many Seniors do choose to take Science classes. 

Math:
Similar to Science, most Seniors have already fulfilled their graduation requirements for math. However, those hoping to pursue a technical career will usually continue to take math, going to the next course in their math lane (most often AP Calculus AB or AP Calculus BC). Some Seniors also take AP Statistics. 

Living Skills:
Many Seniors take Living Skills, since it is a graduation requirement and they didn't take it in previous years. Living Skills can also be taken over the summer as an intensive 3-week course which is only open to rising Seniors.

title: Senior Quad
text:
Gunn Wiki article: Senior Quad

Overview

The Senior Quad is one of the two "quads" (quadrangles, a bit like courtyards) at Gunn. The Senior Quad is generally considered to consist of a slightly elevated area covered by artificial turfing and a set of neat concrete squares topped with wood. There are also a few standard tables surrounding the elevated flat. It is located in front of the P building, and on the WATT Gunn campus map  it is simply labelled as "Quad." The area is a popular spot for upperclassmen during brunch and lunch, as it is located directly in front of the cafeteria in the P building. A wall of trees surrounds it from the side of the E building, providing decent shade on hot days. School wide events, such as the Club Fair, Oktoberfest, and Welcome Back Dance are hosted in this area due to it being the largest paved open area on campus.

Trivia

Despite being one of the two quads, the other being the Freshman Quad, the Gunn WATT app's map says that it's the only quad.

title: Social Justice Pathway

Gunn Wiki article: Social Justice Pathway

The Social Justice Pathway is a course path rising sophomores can opt to take instead of the traditional path. It consists of alternate (more social justice-focused) versions of social studies classes, plus an optional AAR-SJ class. The pathway can be dropped, but generally choosing to enroll as a rising sophomore means a commitment through senior year. The program is organized by Ms. Dellaporta.

US History SJ - replaces US History

title: Sophomore
text:
Gunn Wiki article: Sophomore

A sophomore is a 10th grader.

Course selection:
English:
Sophomores can take English 10 or English 10A.

Social studies:
Sophomores take a semester of Contemporary World History and a semester of US Government (or the Social Justice Pathway equivalents).

Math:
Sophomores who took Algebra 1 the previous year have a choice between Geometry and Geometry H. Students who took Geometry H generally take Algebra 2 + Trig H next, although some go to Algebra 2 + Trig A. Students who took Geometry during their freshman year can choose between Algebra 2 + Trig A and Algebra 2, although some lane up to Algebra 2 + Trig H.

Science:
Sophomores are required to take any physical science course (typically Chemistry or Chemistry Honors), as long as they have the proper math accreditation (this only affects AP Physics 1 and AP Physics C).

PE:
One more year of PE is required, although some students do it during their junior year instead of their sophomore year.

title: Spangenberg Pool
text:
Gunn Wiki article: Spangenberg Pool

There is an indoor pool on the top of Spangenberg Theatre. Few have been able to swim in it due to its tight security, but various pictures have been taken.

The roof over the pool was added in recent years to prevent it from being seen by satellite maps.

Anonymous sources have claimed that Gunn alumni were tasked by the school administration to infiltrate companies such as Google to remove any traces of the pool on their maps.

title: Spangenberg Theater
text:
Gunn Wiki article: Spangenberg Theater

The Spangenberg Theater, or simply Spangenberg, is Gunn's main theater and auditorium. It has a seating capacity of 925 people (915 seats+10 wheelchair spots), which is about half of Gunn's population. It was built in 1964 and was dedicated to Karl Spangenberg on 1964-05-12. 

Function as a school auditorium:
Spangenberg is used to hold many school assemblies, for example expectations talks for Freshmen, Homecoming theme reveal videos, SEC candidate speeches, and other marginally useful school assemblies viewed mainly as a waste of time by students. School plays are also presented here.  

Function as a theater:
The theater is also used to show Gunn Theatre productions, as well as host the annual TEDxGunn High School conference. It is also a performance venue for Gunn's instrumental music program. 

Pool:
A school legend states that there is a pool on top of Spangenberg. This is totally false and there is no reason for anyone to believe it.

title: Spanish 3
text:
Gunn Wiki article: Spanish 3

Key facts: title: Spanish 3; department: lang; length: year; weighted: no

Spanish 3 is the third course and second-last course in Gunn's Spanish progression. Students study grammar and vocabulary and become more comfortable speaking fluidly in preparation of AP Spanish. 

Course Catalog Description:
Level III World Language classes are designed for non-native speakers of the target language. The curriculum prepares students to: perform interpersonal, interpretive and presentational communicative tasks within the intermediate mid- range on the ACTFL Proficiency Guidelines; interpret, exchange, and present information, concepts and ideas both within the classroom and beyond on a variety of topics including connections to other subject areas; and understand the relationship among the products, practices and perspectives of the target culture(s) and other cultures. This course is rather difficult and an A grade is not guaranteed, especially if your only experience in Spanish is from school courses. Take this course if you're interested in furthering your Spanish skills and moving on to AP Spanish.

title: Stanford Chinese School
text:
Gunn Wiki article: Stanford Chinese School

Stanford Chinese school is a Chinese school that holds classes on Saturdays in the N building. It was founded in 1994 by Ma Liping on the Stanford University campus but moved to Gunn in 2001. The students occasionally leave Chinese vocabulary cards, 30 mm squares of card stock with a Chinese word printed on them, lying around. 

Curriculum:
Dr. Ma designed her own curriculum, which is made for "heritage Chinese speakers" (i.e. people who speak Chinese in the household), for the school. This is obvious because both the school and the curriculum's website are mainly in Chinese. Students read various texts both Chinese and western, including Chinese idioms, stories about Afanti, and "The Last Lesson" by Alphonse Daudet. This curriculum is also used in other schools including local afterschool Mustard Seed.

title: Stanford Chinese School
text:
ories about Afanti, and "The Last Lesson" by Alphonse Daudet. This curriculum is also used in other schools including local afterschool Mustard Seed.

Another local afterschool, Acme (which is located at the Cubberly Community Center), uses a curriculum similar to this one, following the same basic structure of instructional texts and homework assigned weekly. However, the texts are rather shallower and more sanitized, talking mainly about occurrences like the first day of school, going to a bookstore, and going to the airport. Also, the curriculum may be described as communist Chinese propaganda, including texts glorifying Chinese Hong Kong while painting British Hong Kong in an unfavorable light, and a text about Mount Everest stating of its geographic location only that it is part of China.

title: Strawberry Hill
text:
Gunn Wiki article: Strawberry Hill

Strawberry Hill is a hill north and slightly west of Gunn High School. Well known by Gunn Track athletes as "gut buster hill" or similar names, the hill is mostly covered in yellow grass. Several concrete paths converge on top of the hill: a path going from Bol Park to the west side of Gunn, a path coming up from the softball and football fields, and a path going alongside the soccer field to another bike path. An unpaved path, sometimes used by runners, cuts through the yellow grass.

Two benches are located at the top of the hill. One is dedicated to Cameron Scott Lee, a Gunn student who took his own life in 2014. The plaque reads: " ... ". The other is dedicated to ..., who was born in Stalingrad and moved to Palo Alto in .... The hill has a single oak tree, which Timothy Herchen notes is covered in oak galls, signifying that the tree is unhealthy.

As of July 2024, the airspace above Strawberry Hill is classified as KNUQ class D airspace, operating UAS without airspace authorization is a violation of 14 CFR § 107.41.

title: Student Activities Center
text:
Gunn Wiki article: Student Activities Center

The Student Activities Center, or SAC, is a room located in the P building used as an interface between SEC and the student body. More specifically, it is used to purchase items, get club posters stamped, turn in club attendance forms, and get information about events in general. 

Things that can be purchased at the SAC include Gunn merchandise, parking passes, and when relevant dance/event tickets, yearbooks, et cetera. 

The SAC also contains a selection of board games, a ping pong table, some comfortable couches, and a copy of almost every Gunn yearbook that's been published since 1967.

Gunn Wiki article: Student Executive Council

SEC is the student government of Gunn. They meet in room P-105 and are responsible for hosting school events and activities. Their official website is www.gunnsec.org.

Positions:
SEC, like many other student governments, has many positions for students to run for (elected) or apply for (appointed). For a list of who is currently in which position in SEC in the 2020-2021 school year, look here.

List of positions:
The School Board Representative is elected at the end of the preceding school year and is a student voice in the PAUSD Board of Education.
The President is the leader of SEC. There is also a Vice President of SEC.
There are class presidents and vice presidents for each class in SEC as well.

title: Student ID
text:
Gunn Wiki article: Student ID

A student ID is an eight-digit number assigned to every PAUSD student. All student IDs in PAUSD start with 950, although there is at least one known misprinted ID card starting with 940.

Uses:
Before the 2020–2021 school year, student IDs were used to sign in to Flex. Teachers use the FlexTime App to mark students as present for Flex, entering student IDs either by typing them in or scanning barcodes on student ID cards, which have the student ID encoded in Code 39.

Student IDs are also used as a username to sign into student services such as the ClassLink. Student IDs are also used to get school-provided meals from the cafeteria, and utilised by SEC to charter clubs. As of the 2025-2026 school year, Student IDs are also used to sign in to classrooms to allow automatic tracking of attendance and the use of the online hall pass system. 

School-issued emails are of the form FLXXXXX@pausd.us, where F is the student's first initial, L the last initial, and XXXXX the last five digits of the student ID (i.e. excluding 950).

title: Student ID Card
text:
Gunn Wiki article: Student ID Card

A student ID card is an identification card issued to PAUSD students at the beginning of each school year. It lists each student's school, grade, student ID number, and library card number. It also includes the student's most recent school (yearbook) photo and a barcode of their student ID. 

The main use of student ID cards is as a quickly scannable card used to enter students into a database, for example when checking out textbooks or in the brunch and lunch lines. They are also used during standardized testing (for example the AP tests or the PSAT) to verify student identity. 

Lost your ID?:
Losing a student ID is a fairly common occurrence. Lost student IDs are supposed to be turned in at the SAC; if turned in, they can be picked up there.  Students can also use the barcode generation feature on WATT for things like the lunch line, but some more formal procedures like checking in to prom require a physical ID card.

title: Study Hall
text:
Gunn Wiki article: Study Hall

Study Hall is, as the name suggests, a study-hall period that meets every other Friday, alternating with SELF. As it is towards the end of Friday, there are few classes one can use this period to study for, so many students simply play video games during this period.

In the 2024-25 school year, a system allowing students to sign up for different classes through FlexiSched was implemented, similar to PRIME. Before then, students were restricted to their study hall classroom and couldn't leave.

title: Summer School
text:
Gunn Wiki article: Summer School

Summer School refers to a collection of summer programs that behave similarly. Each summer generally has 2 sessions, each of which corresponds to a semester of content, and has roughly the same number of instructional minutes.

Unlike school during the school year, a single school is used for all high schools, alternating between Gunn and Paly.

Credit Recovery:
Students who do not pass a course (and took the course with the intention of getting credit) will automatically be placed in a queue for Credit Recovery by the counselors. Students with a closer graduation year and larger number of deficient credits are prioritized. Students may take 2 classes per session (1 in the morning, 1 in the afternoon), recovering up to 10 credits per session, 20 credits per summer.

Kick-Start:

title: Summer School
text:
ts may take 2 classes per session (1 in the morning, 1 in the afternoon), recovering up to 10 credits per session, 20 credits per summer.

Kick-Start:
Kick-Start allows students to take a course during the summer to free up a period during the following school year. Unlike Credit Recovery, only one Kick-Start course may be taken each session, and it is taken in the morning, with an async afternoon. Students may also take a Credit Recovery course in the afternoon.

Students must explicitly register for Kick-Start slightly after normal course registration finishes, and with certain exceptions, may not use the freed up period for anything besides a Prep.

Kick-Start does not exist in 2022 due to COVID-19 and fewer staff members.

Special courses:
While Living Skills and Economics technically fall under Kick-Start, their popularity has led them to be registered for separately. Both of these are limited to rising seniors, and may not meet at the same time as the rest of summer school.

Finally, PAUSD offers a number of non-credit courses during the summer, registered for the same way Kick-Start courses are registered for. Instead of focusing on academics, they cover summer camp-like content, providing access to families who cannot afford private summer camps.

The Symphonic Band is an advanced ensemble open to students with a strong instrumental background who wish to be part of a quality performing group. There will be an emphasis on performance techniques and developing a repertoire of the finest literature for performances. As a result of this experience, the student will be able to better express themselves creatively, and they will have a knowledge and appreciation of music history. Both performance and written assessments will be included in the curriculum.

The Symphonic Band is an ensemble committed to a high level of study and performances of standard and contemporary large band repertoire. This ensemble provides the students with the opportunity to study and perform outstanding band literature from the renaissance to the present.

TEDxGunnHighSchool, sometimes abbreviated to TEDx, is an annual TEDx event run by the club of the same name. According to the TED website, TEDx is "a grassroots initiative, created in the spirit of TED’s overall mission to research and discover 'ideas worth spreading.' TEDx brings the spirit of TED to local communities around the globe through TEDx events. These events are organized by passionate individuals who seek to uncover new ideas and to share the latest research in their local areas that spark conversations in their communities." Event:
TEDx is an all-day event that occurs every year, usually on a Monday around February. It is broken up into two halves (before and after lunch); students can choose to attend one or both halves and are excused from classes during the time they sign up for. Some teachers will also choose for their whole class to attend the event during their class period.

title: The Oracle
text:
Gunn Wiki article: The Oracle

The Oracle is Gunn's monthly newspaper, available as printed issues and online at gunnoracle.com. It often puts out surveys of student opinion or experience and incorporates the results into articles. It is published by students in the Advanced Journalism and Media Studies - Newspaper class. The Oracle also runs Instagram and Facebook accounts, which publish shorter articles on school events.

Print issue sections:
The Oracle is organized into six main sections, each of which covers a different topic or category of article in each issue. These sections are:

News — reports on local and national events, especially those which affect students.
Forum — opinion pieces about various social issues, usually less "newsworthy" ones, noticed in the community.
In-Depth (previously Centerfold) — just one article, the longest of the issue and over the largest spread (2 pages). Focuses on a single community issue or other topic, usually not "breaking news".

Examples include features on campus supervisors, the Unity PE class, teachers who were previously Gunn students, and student wellness advocates.

title: Titan Broadcast Network
text:
Gunn Wiki article: Titan Broadcast Network

TBN, the Titan Broadcast Network, is the student-run broadcast media organization at Gunn. Its material is produced by students in the Broadcast Journalism (Titan Vision) class. 

In the 2020-2021 school year, they switched from their full-length morning announcement program to a shortened segment called The G. At some point during the pandemic, the program was discontinued, though it restarted as a club in the 2023-2024 school year and as a class in 2024-2025.

Format:
Formerly, a typical TBN program would run for 2 to 6 minutes, including an intro theme. The morning announcements were delivered live by student anchors, usually two, or in a short slideshow presentation on certain days. During the COVID-19 pandemic, TBN started airing a short prerecorded announcement program called The G instead of live announcements.

Now, TBN produces short news reports and posts them to its Instagram page.

https://gunn.pausd.org/connecting/tbn - TBN Official Website

title: Trash
text:
Gunn Wiki article: Trash

Litter is commonly seen outdoors on the Gunn campus. There is at least one set of waste bins (trash, recycling, and compost) in every classroom, as well as many outside around campus. There are very few places on campus that do not have at least one set of waste bins within eyeshot. 

Sorting:
Most of Gunn's garbage cans come in sets of three with landfill, recycling, and compost. Students are encouraged to sort their trash properly, however, this is frequently ignored. Infographics taped to the side of each bin showing which items go where seem to do little to help the situation. 

Attempts to solve:
In 2024, a Social Justice AAR group started a poster campaign to get people to pick up their trash.

In 2025, another Social Justice AAR group conducted a small-scale study that found that greater student-custodian connection led to less littering.

Course catalog description:
This is a course for students who want an advanced program in high school English. This honors-level course uses the works of authors such as Shakespeare, Achebe, Brontë, and Austen to study composition and literature. Additionally, the course utilizes world classics to explore the influence of world culture, thought, and values on contemporary thinking. Because it is a required course, it includes particular emphasis on instruction in reading and writing. Students should expect to complete two to three major essay-quality assignments during the course. One semester of this course or World Literature is required.
